HR@10 with one positive and 99 unique negatives measures ranking within 100 candidates; it does not establish full-catalog top-10 quality. Krichene and Rendle show that sampled ranking metrics can reverse model orderings even in expectation. Keep the pinned evaluator unchanged and describe results as sampled validation HR@10. Pairwise training objectives such as BPR encourage positive-over-negative ordering, but lower loss or larger margins do not guarantee higher HR@10, which changes only when the positive crosses the rank-10 boundary. [Sampled-metric analysis](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/), [BPR](https://arxiv.org/abs/1205.2618).

Repeated hyperparameter and checkpoint selection can overfit a finite validation set: the winning score is optimistically selected, even when training never uses validation labels. Cawley and Talbot find that selection effects can rival differences between learning algorithms. Fixed seeds improve comparability but do not eliminate this uncertainty. Preserve the held-out test for final evaluation and treat small validation improvements cautiously. [Model-selection bias](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v11/cawley10a.html).

Suggested diagnostic: retain each model’s per-user hit indicators and bootstrap paired user differences within each category, then average the four category differences equally. Resample the same users for both models, preserving their fixed candidate sets. This estimates user-sampling uncertainty conditional on the fitted models and candidates; it does not capture training randomness, negative-sampling variability, or correct repeated-selection bias. With 200 users/category, one additional hit changes category HR by 0.005 and the four-category macro average by 0.00125. Bootstrap intervals are established tools for uncertainty in retrieval averages. [Confidence-interval study](https://www.nist.gov/publications/computing-confidence-intervals-common-ir-measures).
